Grapes
grapes
n. pl. (the fruit of the vine; rendering Hebrew anab, Greek staphule)
From Old French grape, a bunch or cluster, originally a hook used in harvesting. The English word names the cluster before the single berry, which is how Scripture almost always speaks of them — a cluster carried, gathered, or trodden.

Biblical Definition

Grapes in Scripture are the fruit by which a vine is judged. The spies bring back the evidence of Canaan: “they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff” (Numbers 13:23) — a cluster requiring two men and a pole, and ten of the twelve who carried it still counselled against going in. Isaiah's song of the vineyard makes grapes the test of a nation: God fenced it, cleared the stones, planted the choicest vine, built a tower and a winepress, “and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2). Everything that could be done had been done; what failed was the fruit, and the chapter names it — he looked for judgment and beheld oppression, for righteousness and beheld a cry. Our Lord uses the same test for teachers: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Matthew 7:16) — the question expects the obvious answer, and Luke gives the same rule from the other side: “every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes” (Luke 6:44). It is the practical test for detecting false prophets. And Revelation uses the harvest for the last judgment: “gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe” (Revelation 14:18). Ripeness is the signal, and the gathering is into the winepress of the wrath of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fruit by which a vine is judged. Eshcol's cluster took two men to carry; Isaiah's vineyard had every advantage and yielded wild grapes; Christ makes fruit the test of teachers; Revelation harvests when the grapes are ripe.

expand to see more

GRAPE, n. [Fr. grappe, a cluster or bunch.] The fruit of the vine, growing in clusters.

2. Grapes are of various colors, and are used for food, and for making wine.

3. A mangy tumor on the legs of a horse.

4. Grape-shot, a cluster of small iron balls confined in a canvas bag.

5. In Scripture, the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim, Judg. 8; sour grapes, Ezek. 18.

Key Scripture

Numbers 13:23 — "And they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff; and they brought of the pomegranates, and of the figs."

Isaiah 5:2 — "And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes."

Luke 6:44 — "For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes."

Revelation 14:18 — "And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe."

Modern Corruption

Teachers are assessed by gifting, popularity, or sincerity rather than by fruit — and Isaiah 5 is read as a general lament instead of the specific charge of injustice it makes.

expand to see more

Matthew 7:16 supplies the church's standing test for teachers, and it is regularly set aside for easier ones. Sincerity is not a fruit — a man may be entirely sincere and be a thornbush. Nor is a crowd a fruit, nor eloquence, nor even orthodoxy recited without a life to match. What our Lord means by fruit is filled out elsewhere: the fruit of the Spirit in a man's character, and the fruit of his doctrine in those who follow him. He puts this test immediately after warning of wolves in sheep's clothing, so the whole point is that appearance and profession will not distinguish them. It takes time to see fruit, which is why 1 Timothy 3 requires a man to be proved and not a novice.

The principle to recover is what Isaiah's vineyard was actually charged with. God had given it everything — a fenced hill, cleared stones, the choicest vine, a tower, a winepress — and looked for grapes. The wild grapes are named in verse 7 and they are not doctrinal errors: he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. The woes that follow fall on those who join house to house and field to field, on those who call evil good and good evil, and on those who justify the wicked for reward. A church with every advantage that produces no justice has produced wild grapes, whatever its confession says.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew anab is a grape or cluster; beushim are wild or worthless grapes; eshkol is a cluster, and the name of the valley. Greek staphule is a bunch of grapes.

expand to see more

Hebrew anab (H6025) — a grape; the fruit looked for in Isaiah's vineyard.

Hebrew beushim (H891) — wild, stinking, worthless grapes; what the vineyard yielded.

Hebrew eshkol (H811) — a cluster; also the name of the brook the spies came to.

Greek staphule (G4718) — a bunch of grapes; do men gather grapes of thorns?

Greek karpos (G2590) — fruit; the test by which teachers are known.

Usage

"Of the cluster carried between two: a branch with one cluster of grapes (Numbers 13:23)."

"Of a vineyard that failed its owner: he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2)."

"Of the test of teachers: do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? (Matthew 7:16)."
